results.title: LLM Agents for Bargaining with Utility-based Feedback | alphaXiv
results.content: Researchers at KAIST AI and LG AI Research introduce BARGAINARENA, a comprehensive benchmark for realistic LLM bargaining, and HAMBA, a human-aligned evaluation metric. They also propose ICL with Utility-based Feedback (ICL-UF), which consistently improved LLM negotiation performance and fostered opponent-aware reasoning. While LLMs have shown promise in various strategic tasks, their performance in complex, real-world negotiation scenarios remains limited due to oversimplified benchmarks and inadequate evaluation metrics that fail to capture human preferences and strategic reasoning. *Figure 1: Overview of the BARGAINARENA framework showing the negotiation process between buyer and seller agents across six different market types (Vanilla, Deceptive, Monopoly, Installment, Negative Perception, and Several Product markets) with various goods categories.*. The paper introduces three key innovations to advance LLM capabilities in bargaining scenarios: a comprehensive benchmark dataset called BARGAINARENA, a human-aligned evaluation metric called HAMBA (Human-Aligned Metric for Bargaining), and an in-context learning approach with utility-based feedback (ICL-UF). These contributions collectively address the gap between current LLM negotiation capabilities and the complexity of real-world market interactions. Existing negotiation benchmarks predominantly focus on simplified, single-issue scenarios that fail to capture the nuanced dynamics of real-world markets. The authors introduce BARGAINARENA, a comprehensive dataset featuring six distinct market types that reflect real-world negotiation complexities:. *Figure 3: Comparison between ICL-UF and baseline ReAct approach, showing how utility-based feedback promotes opponent-aware reasoning versus tactic-centric reasoning.*. *Figure 4: HAMBA scores across different market types and LLM models, demonstrating the effectiveness of ICL-UF (blue bars) compared to baseline approaches.*. 3. **Effective Learning Mechanism**: ICL-UF demonstrates how utility-based feedback can enhance strategic reasoning without requiring extensive model retraining. This research establishes a new standard for evaluating and training LLM agents in strategic negotiation scenarios. By introducing realistic benchmarks, human-aligned metrics, and effective learning mechanisms, the work advances our understanding of how LLMs can be developed to handle complex, multi-faceted interactions that better reflect real-world negotiation dynamics. This paper is cited as foundational work that introduced one of the first benchmark datasets for negotiation dialogues. It serves as a key point of comparison, as the main paper argues that its own end-to-end approach with utility-based feedback is more effective in complex scenarios than this earlier decoupled model.

results.title: Public Goods Game (PGG) AI Benchmark: Contribute & Punish
results.content: # Public Goods Game (PGG) AI Benchmark: Contribute & Punish. How Multiple LLMs Share Resources, Punish Free-Riders, and What It Means for Real-World AI Systems. * LLMs Exhibit Human-Like Negotiation & Retaliation: Our experiments show that Large Language Models can adopt surprisingly social behaviors—threats, alliances, and punishments—when placed in shared-resource settings. * Communication Boosts Cooperation (Temporarily): Allowing models to publicly message each other increases overall contributions initially, though it doesn’t necessarily avert destructive punishment cycles in later rounds. * Implications for AI Governance: Enterprises or teams deploying multiple AI agents must consider how punishment rules, incentives, and communication channels shape collective outcomes, potentially preventing resource depletion or conflict spirals. * Relevance for Business: From resource allocation in a decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) to AI-driven negotiations in supply chains, these findings help leaders design or tune multi-agent AI systems for robust performance and reduced conflict. This scenario parallels the behaviors observed in our Public Goods Game (PGG) Benchmark, where even sophisticated Large Language Models can spiral into feuds if incentives aren’t carefully structured. 1. AI Deployment in Cross-Functional Settings Deploying multiple LLMs for tasks like budget approvals, project prioritization, or resource distribution can benefit from explicit “cooperation architecture” that sets limits on negative feedback loops (punishment) and fosters communication. * Extend or Customize: Researchers and industry teams can alter the multiplication factor, the punishment cost, or the number of tokens and players to simulate domain-specific resource dilemmas—ideal for testing how AI agents might behave under new incentive structures. Our Public Goods Game (PGG) Benchmark: Contribute & Punish reveals that LLMs can display nuanced, “human-like” negotiation, cooperation, and retribution behaviors under repeated interactions. For businesses and researchers, these findings stress the importance of carefully engineering the incentives, punishments, and communication pathways in multi-agent AI systems. By tuning these parameters, organizations can optimize resource sharing, minimize destructive retaliatory spirals, and better align collaborative AI agents with human goals. ### Elimination Game: Measuring Social Reasoning, Strategy, and Deception in LLMs. When LLMs move from single-turn tasks to multi-agent settings, a new question emerges: can they coordinate, persuade…. ### BAZAAR: A New Benchmark for Testing Economic Reasoning in LLMs. As AI moves from generating text to executing real-world tasks, we face a critical question: can AI agents reason….

results.title: Negotiation Dialogues Dataset
results.content: ## **EQ-Negotiator: An Emotion-Reasoning LLM Agent in Credit Dialogues**. Abstract:While large language model (LLM)-based chatbots have been applied for effective engagement in credit dialogues, their capacity for dynamic emotional expression remains limited. This paper introduces an EQ-negotiator that combines emotion sensing from pre-trained language models (PLMs) with emotional reasoning based on Game Theory and Hidden Markov Models. By fine-tuning pre-trained language models (PLMs) on public emotion datasets and validating them on the credit dialogue datasets, our approach enables LLM-based agents to effectively capture shifts in client emotions and dynamically adjust their response tone based on our emotion decision policies in real-world financial negotiations. To address this, we propose the Sentiment Cross-Lingual Recognition and Logic Framework (SentiXRL), which incorporates two modules,an emotion retrieval enhancement module to improve sentiment classification accuracy in complex contexts through historical dialogue and logical reasoning,and a self-circulating analysis negotiation mechanism (SANM)to facilitates autonomous decision-making within a single model for classification tasks.We have validated SentiXRL's superiority on multiple standard datasets, outperforming existing models on CPED and CH-SIMS,and achieving overall better performance on MELD,Emorynlp and IEMOCAP. Authors:Darshan Deshpande, Shambhavi Sinha, Anirudh Ravi Kumar, Debaditya Pal, Jonathan May. Abstract:Language Models have previously shown strong negotiation capabilities in closed domains where the negotiation strategy prediction scope is constrained to a specific setup. Following this, we propose an automated framework called GNOME, which processes existing human-annotated, closed-domain datasets using Large Language Models and produces synthetic open-domain dialogues for negotiation. ## **Assistive Large Language Model Agents for Socially-Aware Negotiation Dialogues**. Abstract:In this paper, we propose a novel negotiation dialogue agent designed for the online marketplace. For this dataset creation, we introduce a new semi-automated data creation method, which combines defining negotiation intents, actions, and intent-action simulation between users and the agent to generate potential dialogue flows. By leveraging the IND, we train our model and conduct experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of our reward-based dialogue system for negotiation. By releasing GPT-Negochat and our baseline models, we aim to encourage further research in multi-issue negotiation dialogue agreement tracking. ## **Opponent Modeling in Negotiation Dialogues by Related Data Adaptation**. ## **Towards Emotion-Aware Agents For Negotiation Dialogues**.
